I measured the flour carefully. Leveled the spoon. Checked every step twice. My grandmother just worked. She pinched dough, added water, adjusted the filling—no measuring cups, no spoons. When I asked how much salt she used, she shrugged. "Enough," she said.

That wasn't the answer I wanted.

The dough felt dry, so I added water. Then it got sticky, so I added more flour. Pretty soon it was tough and lumpy, and the wrappers tore when I tried to fold them. Filling leaked everywhere. I kept fixing one problem after another, but each fix just made a new one.

By dinner, my dumplings looked like sad little envelopes. Nothing like hers. I was embarrassed. I'd followed the recipe, made careful adjustments, and still messed up. My grandmother picked one up, tasted it, and smiled. "It tastes good," she said.

She wasn't wrong. But I was upset because I wanted to get it right the first time. I thought mistakes meant I hadn't paid enough attention or tried hard enough. If I just prepared more, measured better, eliminated uncertainty—I could avoid failing.

My grandmother saw it differently. She asked me to make dumplings with her again the next week. This time, no recipe. Just notice how the dough feels. Crumbly? Add a little water. Too sticky? Add a small amount of flour. Then wait and see.

The second batch was still imperfect. I added too much water at first, and one wrapper split before I could fill it. But I stopped trying to fix everything at once. I worked with what was in front of me, made small adjustments, paid attention. When a dumpling fell apart, I looked at why. The wrapper was too thin in the center. So I rolled the next one more evenly.

By the end, they weren't identical, but they held together. And I understood the process better than when I'd followed the recipe perfectly.

That changed how I handle mistakes outside the kitchen too. In science class, I ran an experiment that contradicted my hypothesis. My first instinct was to find a way to make the data fit what I expected. Instead, I went back through my procedure, checked my measurements, asked what the unexpected result might mean. I found an error in one step—but I also found that a variable I'd dismissed actually mattered. My mistake didn't just slow me down. It gave me a better question to investigate.

I still care about doing things well. I still prepare and feel disappointed when my work falls short. But a mistake isn't a verdict on my ability anymore. It's information. It tells me what I misunderstood, what I need to practice, what I hadn't considered. That shift makes me more willing to try things I'm not sure I can do.

My grandmother never gave me the exact measurements I wanted. She taught me to pay attention, adjust, and try again. Growth doesn't come from getting everything right immediately. It comes from staying curious when something goes wrong and being willing to change course. I still make uneven dumplings. But the imperfect ones teach me the most.

If you drive far enough into north County Kerry, the road flattens toward the Shannon. Ballyheigue comes in from one side, Lixnaw from the other, and between them is Causeway. A driver might not notice it at all. The place doesn’t announce itself. It isn’t even much of a village by modern standards. It’s a crossroads with a few buildings gathered around it.

Stop, though, and Causeway has an odd, intact feel. A photograph from the 1870s would be hard to dismiss. The same rooflines sit in the same places. The chimneys still stand in the same groups. A visitor from that century could find the pub on roughly the same corner. The street corners look like they were laid out for people on foot and men with carts, not for the kind of traffic that would need lights or a bypass.

The centre is still that junction. Low stone buildings lean into it. There’s a pub or two on the corners, their signs faded by the wind that comes straight over the fields from the Atlantic. Nearby is a grocery or hardware shop, the kind of place that would still sell rope, nails, tea, and a small packet of crisps if someone came in needing all four. The threshold is worn down. You can tell. There are no chain stores here, no bright petrol station canopy, no craft shop selling “authentic” souvenirs. The shops exist because people need them, not because they fit a tourist route.

That’s what makes Causeway strange. Most of Ireland has been rewritten over the last thirty years. Market towns have been widened, bypassed, and filled with retail parks. Causeway hasn’t. It wasn’t protected by law. It was left alone because it was far enough away, small enough, and poor enough to be overlooked.

The land around it is made of small farms and scattered houses. There has never been enough people to make the place grow. The pub conversation carries on across generations. Shopkeepers know who’s who. Some debts are probably still kept in heads rather than computers, or in notebooks that would embarrass a bank. Travellers on the Wild Atlantic Way sometimes drift in and look a little let down. They expect the polished version: rustic gift shop, coffee machine, car park with a machine. Causeway refuses all that. In return, it gives you something harder to find: a place that hasn’t been dressed up for visitors.

Still, quiet places aren’t simple. Young people leave for Tralee, Limerick, Dublin, London. They go for school, work, or just because there isn’t enough going on. The question of whether Causeway will still look like Causeway in fifty years sits over it like low cloud, and not everyone in the village would call that charming. Some of them would prefer a better bus, faster broadband, a job near home.

The leaving isn’t new. People went out, came back, died, married, sold the farm, stayed anyway. The roads changed, but the pattern didn’t.

For now, Causeway goes on at its own speed. It is a crossroads that never became anything more than a crossroads. Cars pass through, and the shop door stays open until someone needs something from it.

Anonymous workplace surveys aren't as anonymous as they look. The tool might strip your name, but that doesn't mean nobody can figure out who said what.

Start with demographics. Surveys ask for your department, team, tenure, job level, location. All that slicing makes results useful for management. It also makes you findable. If your team has four people and you're the only recent hire, a comment like "as someone who transferred here in March" is a name tag. HR and execs often read verbatim comments. Even with good intentions, patterns jump out. A writing style. A project name. A complaint only one person could have made. The smaller the group, the more careful you should be.

Then there's the tool itself. Some platforms track who responded separately from what they said. Fine in theory. But metadata leaks. Timestamps. IP addresses. An export with respondent IDs still attached. If a vendor runs the survey, ask how responses are stored and who sees raw data. If HR runs it internally, remember HR works for management. It's not a confessional. Real anonymity needs safeguards: a third-party admin, aggregate-only reporting with minimum group sizes (usually five or more), no free text stored next to identifying details. Can't verify any of that? Assume partial anonymity at best.

Even when nobody can identify you, your answers do things. Survey results drive decisions. Report a serious problem and management might investigate a specific incident. The pool of plausible complainers could be tiny. Or a manager gets wind of low morale and spends the next month on damage control, morale theater, trying to sniff out who's unhappy instead of fixing anything. Bad reactions to aggregate results can poison a whole team.

There's also strategy at play. Surveys get used to evaluate managers, justify reorgs, support decisions about layoffs, pay, office policy. Your honest answers feed decisions made by people whose interests aren't yours. Say "everything's fine" when it isn't, and you've suppressed the information that might have forced change. Tell the truth about a toxic manager and you might trigger a process that hurts you if it isn't genuinely protected. Figure out whether the survey is real feedback or box-checking. The value of honesty depends on which.

And surveys are rarely your only option, or your best one. Got a serious concern? Raise it directly, in writing, through a real channel. Your manager, skip-level, HR, a hotline. That's on the record in a way you control. An anonymous survey gives you no chance to follow up, clarify, or defend yourself if someone misreads your comment.

So: be honest about general opinions and mild criticism. That's what surveys are for. Be careful with free text, specific incidents, anything that identifies you through context. Skip sarcasm and hyperbole, they read badly out of context. Never write anything you'd hate to hear read aloud in a meeting with your name on it. Treat "anonymous" as "possibly identifiable" until proven otherwise. Honesty matters. Just match how specific and sensitive you get to how much protection you actually have.

One thing I wish I’d known when I started: whatever approach you choose, don’t go all-out from day one. Leave yourself room to improve.

I see it here and at the gym all the time. Someone dives in headfirst—runs until they’re sick, takes every set to failure, signs up for six HIIT classes a week. They feel great for a couple of weeks. Then their knees start hurting, they lose motivation, or they stop making progress and quit. It’s not that they lack discipline. They’ve picked an intensity they can’t sustain, with nowhere to go once their body adjusts.

Your body adapts to training. That’s the point, and early on, it can adapt quickly. But it also means the workout that crushed you in January might feel like a warm-up by March. If you started at full effort, your next step is usually more volume, more sessions, or just more discomfort. That can lead to burnout or injury. Start at 70–80% of what you can manage, and you’ll have months to make steady, satisfying progress before you need to rethink your plan.

This applies to just about everything. New to running? Don’t start with daily 5Ks at race pace. Try three easy runs a week at a pace where you can still talk, then build from there. Starting to lift? Keep a few reps in reserve and add weight gradually. Save the all-out sets for when they’re useful. Taking a class or following a home program? Modify the exercises if you need to. Nobody’s judging, and the people who stick with it are usually the ones who pace themselves.

The people who change their bodies aren’t necessarily the ones who train hardest in week one. They’re the ones still showing up and making progress a year later. Leaving yourself some headroom helps you stay in it.

One other thing, since this comes up a lot: if you want feedback on a program or advice in this sub, be specific. “How do I get fit?” tends to get vague answers. “I’m 36, weigh 190 pounds, can run a 5K in 31 minutes, and want to get that down to 25 by June while lifting three days a week. Here’s my current plan.” That gives people something useful to work with.

Making Minetest accessible to a broader audience has been a focus. Ahola noted that the team wants the game to run well on older hardware, so people with less powerful computers can still play. The engine supports a range of platforms, including Windows, macOS, Linux, and some mobile devices.

No, ignoring true north isn’t automatically bad. It depends on what you’re doing. For most hiking, backpacking, and casual day-trip navigation, you can leave it alone. Magnetic declination—the gap between true north and magnetic north—ranges from near zero to over 20 degrees, depending on where you are. At 10 degrees, if you walk a mile on a raw bearing, you’ll end up about 920 feet off target. That sounds alarming until you remember most hikers are using trails, ridgelines, rivers, and obvious landmarks, not marching on exact bearings for miles. If you’re just orienting a map and taking rough bearings toward something you can see, the error barely matters. A 20-degree miss over a quarter mile is only around 300 feet, and you can usually fix it by looking ahead.

Where it actually gets risky is when small errors can pile up. Long off-trail travel in desert, tundra, or thick forest is one. Winter mountaineering and whiteouts are another, because there’s nothing to aim at. And if you’re trying to hit a specific water source or campsite on a precise bearing, declination matters. In those cases, ignoring it can put you somewhere else entirely.

Fixing it isn’t hard. Check the declination for your area before you go. It’s usually on the map and online. If your compass has an adjustable declination scale, set it; otherwise, just add or subtract the number when taking bearings. People use “east is least, west is best” for converting magnetic to true, though it’s easy to flip the logic in your head. The real mistake isn’t skipping the correction. It’s not knowing your local declination and when it can bite you. Two degrees? Ignore it. Fifteen degrees? Don’t.
